title: Closures & Anonymous Functions
summary: An **anonymous function** is a function with no name, written inline. A **closure** is such a function that *captures* variables from the enclosing scope by reference, keeping them alive and shared. Closures power callbacks, deferred cleanup, stateful generators, and middleware — but capturing by reference is also the source of one of Go's most famous bugs.

subtopics.title: Anonymous functions are values
subtopics.explanation: A function literal like func(x int) int { return x*x } is a first-class value: you can assign it to a variable, pass it as an argument, return it, or call it immediately. Functions are types in Go, so they fit anywhere a func type is expected.
subtopics.example: sq := func(x int) int { return x * x }; sq(4)

subtopics.title: Closures capture by reference
subtopics.explanation: When an anonymous function refers to a variable from its enclosing scope, it captures that variable itself, not a copy of its value. All closures over the same variable see and mutate the SAME storage, and the variable lives as long as any closure that uses it.

subtopics.title: Stateful closures
subtopics.explanation: Because the captured variable persists, a closure can hold private, mutable state across calls — a counter, an accumulator, a memoization cache. This is the idiomatic way to make a stateful function without a struct.
subtopics.example: func counter() func() int { n:=0; return func() int { n++; return n } }

subtopics.title: The loop-variable capture bug
subtopics.explanation: Before Go 1.22, a for-loop's variable was shared across all iterations, so closures capturing it (especially in goroutines) all saw the final value. Go 1.22 changed loop variables to be per-iteration, fixing the common case. To be version-safe, pass the value as a parameter or shadow it (v := v).
subtopics.example: for _, v := range items { v := v; go func(){ use(v) }() }

subtopics.title: Closures and defer
subtopics.explanation: A deferred closure reads captured variables at the time it runs (at return), not when it was deferred — unlike a deferred call's arguments, which are evaluated immediately. This is why deferring a closure lets you observe the final value of a variable.
subtopics.example: defer func(){ fmt.Println(x) }() // reads x at return time

subtopics.title: Escape analysis & lifetime
subtopics.explanation: If a closure outlives the function that created it (e.g. it's returned), the captured variables 'escape' to the heap so they stay valid. The compiler's escape analysis decides this automatically; it's why closures can safely hold state but may add small allocations.
subtopics.example: return func() int { n++; return n } // n escapes to the heap

foundations.overview: Functions in Go are first-class values: you can store them, pass them, and return them. An anonymous function is just a function written without a name, inline where you need it. It becomes a closure when it refers to variables declared outside itself — at that point it 'closes over' those variables, capturing them by reference so they stay alive and shared. This single mechanism underlies callbacks, deferred cleanup, HTTP middleware, stateful generators, and functional options. It's also behind the infamous loop-variable bug, so understanding capture semantics is essential.
foundations.formalDefinition: An anonymous function is a function literal with no identifier. A closure is a function value together with references to the variables from its lexical scope that it uses; those captured variables are shared by reference and live as long as the closure does.
foundations.whyItMatters: Closures are pervasive in idiomatic Go — every defer func(){}, every http.HandlerFunc, every functional option, every callback. Misunderstanding capture-by-reference causes subtle, hard-to-spot bugs (especially with goroutines), and 'explain closures and the loop-variable trap' is a near-guaranteed interview question.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a closure as a backpack the function carries: when you create it, you don't copy the items (variables) into the backpack — you tuck in references to the actual lockers where they live. Every closure with the same locker reference sees the same contents, and the lockers stay rented as long as someone holds a reference. Change the locker's contents through one closure and the others see it too.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The compiler runs escape analysis: variables captured by a closure that outlives its enclosing function are allocated on the heap so they remain valid; otherwise they can stay on the stack. A closure value is a small struct: a pointer to the function code plus pointers to the captured variables. Calling it is a normal indirect call. This is why closures are cheap but not free — they can add heap allocations.
foundations.realWorldUsage: http.HandleFunc wraps a closure as a handler; middleware returns a closure wrapping the next handler; sort.Slice takes a comparison closure; functional options (func(*Config)) configure constructors; defer func(){} closes over named returns for recover.
foundations.businessImpact: Closures keep configuration and behavior local and composable (middleware chains, options), which speeds development. But capture bugs that ship to production cause data corruption and incidents, so correctness here protects reliability.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Closures enable clean functional patterns — middleware, callbacks, options — without boilerplate structs. The cost is that capture semantics must be understood team-wide to avoid the loop-variable and shared-state traps.
foundations.performanceImpact: Captured variables that escape are heap-allocated, adding GC pressure if you create many closures in hot loops. The call itself is a cheap indirect call. For extreme hot paths, prefer passing values explicitly or reusing closures to limit allocations.
commonUseCases: HTTP middleware that wraps the next handler in a closure
Functional options: func(*Config) passed to constructors

commonMisconceptions.myth: A closure captures a copy of the variable's value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It captures the variable itself by reference; all closures over it share and can mutate the same storage.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The loop-variable bug still bites in all Go versions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go 1.22+ gives each iteration its own loop variable, fixing the common case; pre-1.22 it was shared. Pass as a parameter or shadow (v:=v) to be version-safe.
Captured variables that escape the creating function are heap-allocated, which can add GC pressure if you make many in hot paths.

config.intro: counter() returns a closure that increments a private n. Step through what happens:

steps.name: Create the variable
steps.detail: Inside counter(), n := 0 is declared. It will be captured by the closure we're about to return.

steps.name: Return the closure
steps.detail: counter returns func() int { n++; return n }. Because this closure uses n and outlives counter, n escapes to the heap.

steps.name: counter() has returned
steps.detail: Normally n would be gone, but the closure holds a reference to it, so the heap keeps n alive.

steps.name: First call
steps.detail: Calling the closure runs n++ on that shared storage and returns 1.

steps.name: State persists
steps.detail: The next call increments the SAME n to 2, and so on — the closure carries private, mutable state between calls.

interactiveExamples.title: A stateful counter via closure
interactiveExamples.explanation: counter returns a closure that captures n by reference. Each call mutates the same n, so the count persists. Two separate counters get independent n's, because each call to counter() makes a fresh variable.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: fix the loop-variable capture (version-safe)
interactiveExamples.explanation: On Go versions before 1.22 all goroutines capture the same loop variable and may print the last value three times. Make this correct on ANY version by passing v as an argument (or shadowing v := v).

checkpoints.explanation: All three closures capture the same variable x by reference. Calling each one runs x++ on that shared storage, so after three calls x is 3.

checkpoints.prompt: How does a closure capture a variable from its enclosing scope?
options: By copying its value at creation time
By reference — it shares the actual variable, which stays alive while the closure does
checkpoints.explanation: Closures capture variables by reference: they refer to the same storage, can mutate it, and keep it alive (escaping to the heap if the closure outlives the enclosing function). They do not snapshot a copy.

checkpoints.prompt: On Go 1.21 (pre-1.22), what does this most likely print and why?
options: 3 3 3 (the closures share i, which is 3 after the loop)
checkpoints.explanation: On pre-1.22 Go the single loop variable i is shared by all three closures. By the time the deferred closures run (at function return), the loop has finished and i is 3, so it prints '3 3 3 '. Capture per iteration with i := i or pass i as an argument. (Note: a deferred CALL like defer fmt.Print(i) would instead capture each value, since arguments are evaluated immediately.)

codeLab.title: A memoizing closure
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Memoize(fn func(int) int) func(int) int` that returns a closure caching results: on a repeated input it returns the cached value instead of calling fn again. The cache is private state captured by the closure.
hints: Declare cache := make(map[int]int) before returning the closure so it's captured.
Inside the closure, check the cache first; on a hit return immediately.
On a miss, call fn(n) once, store the result in the cache, and return it.

debuggingLab.title: All goroutines print the same value
debuggingLab.symptom: This pre-Go-1.22 code is meant to print 0,1,2 (in some order) but prints '3 3 3'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Before Go 1.22 the loop variable i is a single variable shared across all iterations. Each goroutine's closure captures that same i by reference. By the time the goroutines run, the loop has incremented i to 3, so every closure reads 3. (Go 1.22+ makes i per-iteration and prints 0,1,2.)
commonMistakes: Capturing a loop variable in a closure that runs later (goroutine/defer) on pre-1.22 Go.
Assuming the closure snapshots the value rather than the variable.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Give each goroutine its own copy of i — works on every Go version.

theory.question: What is a closure, and how does Go capture variables in one?
theory.directAnswer: A closure is an anonymous function value bundled with references to the variables it uses from its enclosing lexical scope. Go captures those variables by reference, not by value: every closure over the same variable shares the same storage and can mutate it, and the variable stays alive as long as any closure references it (escaping to the heap if it outlives the function that created it). This is what lets closures hold private, persistent state between calls.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A function value plus the captured environment of variables it references.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To enable callbacks, stateful generators, middleware, and functional options without explicit state-holding structs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler records pointers to captured variables in the closure; escape analysis heap-allocates any that outlive their scope so they remain valid.

theory.whyImportant: Capture-by-reference is the crux of both closures' power and their famous bugs; it's a standard interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A counter() that returns func() int { n++; return n } yields a function with private state n that persists across calls.

followUps.question: Do two closures from the same call share state?
followUps.answer: If they capture the same variable, yes — they share its storage. Separate calls to the enclosing function create separate variables and thus independent state.

followUps.question: What does escape analysis have to do with closures?
followUps.answer: It decides whether captured variables must live on the heap (when the closure outlives its creator) versus the stack, which affects allocations.

theory.question: Explain the loop-variable capture bug and how Go 1.22 changed it.
theory.directAnswer: Before Go 1.22, a for-loop used a single loop variable reused across all iterations. A closure created in the loop (often launched as a goroutine or deferred) captured that one shared variable by reference, so by the time it ran the variable held its final value — classic symptom: all goroutines print the last value. Go 1.22 changed the semantics so each iteration gets its own copy of the loop variable, fixing the common case. To be correct on any version, pass the variable as a function argument or shadow it with v := v inside the loop body.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A capture pitfall where deferred or concurrent closures all see a loop variable's final value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Closures capture by reference, and pre-1.22 the loop variable was a single shared storage location.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Go 1.22 makes the loop variable per-iteration, so each closure captures a distinct variable; explicit copying achieves the same on older versions.

theory.whyImportant: It's one of the most famous Go bugs and a frequent interview and code-review topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A worker loop spawning a goroutine per item printed the last item three times on Go 1.21 until the value was passed as a parameter.

followUps.question: Does the bug affect a deferred call's arguments too?
followUps.answer: No — defer fmt.Println(i) evaluates i immediately (capturing the value), whereas defer func(){ fmt.Println(i) }() captures the variable and sees the final value.

followUps.question: How do you write loop closures safely regardless of Go version?
followUps.answer: Pass the loop value as a parameter to the closure, or add v := v at the top of the loop body to create a fresh per-iteration variable.

scenario.question: You want each route handler to share a database pool and a logger without using package-level globals. How do closures help, and what's the risk?
scenario.directAnswer: Build handlers as closures that capture the dependencies: a constructor like makeHandler(db, log) returns an http.HandlerFunc closing over db and log, so each request handler has access without globals — clean dependency injection. The same pattern builds middleware that wraps the next handler in a closure. The risk is shared mutable state: if the captured values are mutated concurrently across requests (each request runs in its own goroutine), you get data races. Capture immutable dependencies, or guard any shared mutable state with a mutex.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Using closures for dependency injection and middleware instead of globals.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Closures let handlers carry their dependencies as captured state, improving testability and avoiding globals.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A factory function returns a handler closure that references the injected dependencies; the HTTP server calls it per request, each in its own goroutine.

scenario.whyImportant: Closure-based handlers and middleware are idiomatic in Go web services, and the concurrency risk is a real production concern.
scenario.realWorldExample: func makeHandler(db *DB) http.HandlerFunc { return func(w, r) { db.Query(...) } } injects db without a global; the *DB pool is safe for concurrent use, but a captured plain map would need locking.

followUps.question: How would you write logging middleware as a closure?
followUps.answer: func WithLogging(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return http.HandlerFunc(func(w,r){ log(...); next.ServeHTTP(w,r) }) } — the closure captures next.

followUps.question: Why prefer this over package globals?
followUps.answer: Captured dependencies are explicit, swappable in tests, and scoped, avoiding hidden global coupling and init-order problems.

coding.question: Implement a rate-limiting style 'once per N calls' wrapper: `Every(n int, fn func()) func()` returns a function that calls fn only on every nth invocation (the 1st, (n+1)th, ...).
coding.thoughtProcess: We need state that persists across calls — a call counter — which is exactly what a closure provides. Capture a counter variable; on each invocation increment it (with modular logic) and call fn only when the counter hits a multiple of n. Capturing by reference keeps the counter alive between calls.
coding.lineByLine: Every guards n>=1, then declares count, the private state the returned closure captures. Each call checks count%n==0: at count 0 (the very first call) and every nth call after, it invokes fn. Then it increments count. Because the closure captures count by reference, the counter survives and advances between calls — no struct or global needed.

followUps.question: Is this safe to call from multiple goroutines?
followUps.answer: No — concurrent calls race on count. Guard it with a sync.Mutex or use an atomic counter if it must be concurrency-safe.

followUps.question: How would you reset it?
followUps.answer: Return a second closure (or a struct) that sets count back to 0; both would capture the same count variable.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Use closures for dependency injection (handler/middleware factories that capture db, logger, config) instead of globals, and for functional options (func(*Config)) that keep constructors flexible. Keep captured dependencies immutable where possible.
productionDeepDive.performance: Closures that escape heap-allocate their captured variables; creating many in hot loops adds GC pressure. Hoist closures out of loops or pass values explicitly on hot paths, and check escape analysis with go build -gcflags=-m when it matters.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A closure shared across goroutines that mutates captured state is a data race — guard shared mutable captures with a mutex or use per-goroutine copies. Always pass loop values as parameters for version-safe goroutine launches and run tests with -race.
productionDeepDive.reliability: The loop-variable capture trap silently produces wrong results; standardize on passing loop values as parameters (or v := v) so behavior is identical across Go versions and reviewers can't miss it.
productionDeepDive.observability: Closures used as middleware are a natural place to add logging, metrics, and tracing that wrap every handler uniformly without touching business logic.
productionDeepDive.security: Be careful what closures capture — capturing secrets or request-scoped data in a long-lived closure can leak it across requests; capture only what's needed and for the right lifetime.

caseStudies.problem: Handlers needed shared dependencies and cross-cutting behavior without globals.
caseStudies.solution: Handler factories and middleware implemented as closures capturing dependencies and the next handler.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Captured mutable state must be concurrency-safe since each request runs in its own goroutine.
caseStudies.lessons: Closures give clean DI and composable middleware, but capture immutable or synchronized state.

caseStudies.problem: Goroutines launched in loops processed the wrong item due to shared loop-variable capture.
caseStudies.solution: Passed the loop value as a parameter (or shadowed it); later upgraded to Go 1.22 per-iteration variables.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Required a code-wide convention until the upgrade.
caseStudies.lessons: Capture-by-reference plus deferred execution is the root cause; explicit per-iteration copies are the robust fix.

keyTakeaways: Anonymous functions are first-class values; a closure is one that captures enclosing variables by reference, sharing and keeping them alive.
Because capture is by reference, closures can hold private persistent state (counters, caches) — and multiple closures over the same variable mutate the same storage.
The loop-variable capture bug (pre-Go 1.22) made deferred/goroutine closures see the final value; pass the value as a parameter or use v := v to be version-safe.

Captured variables that outlive their function escape to the heap; closures power middleware, callbacks, and functional options but need synchronization when shared mutable state is captured across goroutines.
